newsitem.title: KENYA: IMF aid halt scares investors in Kenya, hits economy.
newsitem.headline: IMF aid halt scares investors in Kenya, hits economy.

text.p: International investors' confidence in Kenya's economy took a severe beating on Friday after an International Monetary Fund (IMF) decision to halt a huge aid package because of concern over corruption.

After watching four years of radical economic reforms under the guidance of the IMF and the World Bank, investors woke up on Friday to an apparent vote of no confidence in Kenya as a desirable investment destination.

"We expect a lack of new investments without which the economy cannot grow and produce jobs for the increasing population," said Charles Gardner, resident representative of the Eastern Africa Association that groups British companies.

"We are part of that global market place and so any departure from the IMF programme is going to impact the economy," said John Munge, managing director at leading brokerage house Shah, Munge & Partners.

Gardner said business understood why the IMF was worried. "We share concern with the IMF over corruption and the lack of success in bringing any of the culprits to justice. Corruption distorts the playing field for honest business operators."
A leading investment adviser told Reuters the IMF ruling had a bad effect on Kenya because it meant short-term investors would leave immediately and run elsewhere.
He said such investors were people who did not understand the country well and came on the basis of the IMF programme as well as good yields on government securities.
"An IMF programme for them is absolutely fundamental. It's an absolute requirement, so that's bad," he said, putting potential losses at $200-300 million.
Investors have flooded into Kenya since 1993, when the government began to liberalise in earnest and interest rates as high as 84 percent offered unusually high returns.
Previously, trade and currency trading were controlled and traders could not repatriate their money at will. All that changed in 1993 and foreign cash began flowing to Nairobi.

The IMF said a $205 million three-year loan, offered under its Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF), would lapse on Thursday because the response of President Daniel arap Moi's government to a July 24 deadline had been inadequate. It cited concern about corruption and reform of the energy sector.

Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi said he had expected $215 million this financial year from the IMF and other donors, and said he would cut spending and take revenue measures sufficient to address the $141 million shortfall in external funding.

Foreign investors withdrew from the Nairobi Stock Exchange after the decision, selling 250 million shillings ($4.1 million) of the fourth issue of the Central Bank of Kenya floating-rate treasury bond compared with sales of only 13.35 million shillings in the whole of last week, bourse officials said.
A senior broker warned: "Don't be so sure that Kenya can survive without the IMF aid." Overseas investors account for 40 to 50 percent of business on the Nairobi bourse.

A European investment adviser said investor confidence had already been damaged by political tension following pressure for constitutional reform. He expected the IMF decision to have a ripple effect across the region because Kenya is usually used as a regional base.
Mudavadi began carrying out economic reforms in April 1993, responding to earlier pressure from the IMF, which suspended the supply of funds in 1991 to press for economic and political reforms.
Kenya liberalised foreign exchange trading rules, freed interest rates, streamlined the civil service and started a privatisation process, all of which made Kenya attractive to foreign investors.

The privatisation of the state utility Kenya Posts & Telecommunications Corp and the commercialisation of the Kenya Power & Lighting Company were next in line. The degree of investor interest in the two firms was not clear.
